unit.title: Utilitarianism and its critiques
unit.needIt: This helps you decide if an action is right by looking at the total happiness it creates for everyone. It helps you weigh choices like whether a small personal sacrifice is worth a big gain for a group.
unit.why: A teacher shows how different people react to a choice between personal comfort and the happiness of others. Some people choose their own comfort, while others feel a moral duty to help the group. The lecture explores how these choices define our moral rules.
unit.outcome: Evaluate the morality of actions based on their consequences for the community.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you decide if a small personal inconvenience is worth helping a friend. You also face it when thinking about how your daily habits might affect people far away.
unit.do: Think about one small thing you do every day that helps others. Ask yourself if you would still do it if it cost you a little bit of your own comfort.

quiz.q: What is the goal of moral philosophy?
quiz.why: The lecture states that moral philosophy is the systematic endeavor to understand and justify moral principles.
quiz.quote: What moral philosophy is, is the systematic endeavor to understand moral concepts and to justify moral principles and theories.

quiz.q: Does moral philosophy aim to tell us how people act?
quiz.why: The lecture clarifies that moral theory is a normative enterprise, meaning it looks at how people ought to act.
quiz.quote: Philosophical moral theory doesn't aim to tell us how people act. It aims to tell us how people ought to act in order to wish to conform to the constraints that morality places on them.

quiz.q: What is a self-interest account of morality?
choices: Acting for the good of others
Acting for personal harmony or stability
quiz.why: The lecture explains that self-interest can mean harmony in the soul or stability in society.
quiz.quote: So one category of answers that one might give to why it is that we would be moral, acting keeping with the constraints of morality, is a self-interest account.

quiz.q: What is the core of utilitarianism?
quiz.why: Utilitarianism is a form of consequentialism where the rightness of an act is determined by its results.
quiz.quote: The degree of moral rightness of an act is determined by consequences.

quiz.q: What is the greatest happiness principle?
choices: Follow the rules of the state
quiz.why: Mill defines actions as right if they promote happiness for all concerned.
quiz.quote: Mill says famously, actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to promote the reverse of happiness.

quiz.q: What does Mill say about the motive of an action?
choices: It is the most important part
It tells us nothing about the morality
It only matters for religious acts
quiz.why: Mill argues that the moral value of an act is independent of the reason why it was done.
quiz.quote: The motivation with which an act is performed, says Mill, tells us nothing about the morality of the act.

partials: Moral philosophy is a normative enterprise.
Utilitarianism is a type of consequentialism.
Mill says motives do not change an act's morality.
The goal is to maximize happiness for all.
Actions are right if they promote happiness.
crystal.key: Utilitarianism judges the morality of an act by the total happiness it produces for everyone.

decoys.text: Utilitarianism focuses on the character of the person acting.
decoys.why: The lecture says utilitarianism looks at consequences, not the actor (which is virtue ethics).

decoys.text: Mill believes motives are the most important part of morality.
decoys.why: The lecture states Mill thinks the motive tells us nothing about the morality of the act.

crystal.aha: By looking at the results instead of the person or the reason, utilitarianism provides a systematic way to measure the 'good' of any action.
